Boards whose only USB port is the chip's native USB-Serial-JTAG (Seeed Studio
XIAO ESP32-S3, many ESP32-C3/C6 mini boards) need the console on
USB-Serial-JTAG, otherwise you see no output:

```bash
cd firmware/receiver
idf.py -D SDKCONFIG_DEFAULTS="sdkconfig.defaults;sdkconfig.defaults.usbjtag" set-target esp32s3
idf.py -p /dev/cu.usbmodemXXXX flash monitor

`set-target` regenerates `sdkconfig` from the defaults files. If you change
target or console type, delete `sdkconfig` (or run `set-target` again).

confirmation (never use it on the third board you want to keep):

```bash

Exit `idf.py monitor` with `Ctrl-]` before running `make monitor`; only one

Now I'm digging into FEAT-002's details, starting with the Kconfig changes.

I'm also planning the periodic gain status print, how the host parser and engine will consume it, the optional CSI shift config, and the firmware README updates needed for the reflash instructions. Moving to FEAT-003, I'm starting to track raw amplitude resolution over the processing window.

Now I'm adding quantization detection fields to the MotionFrame — raw median amplitude, zero fraction, and a low-resolution flag — without turning them into a quality gate, plus the status message warning users when CSI values are too coarse and advising a reflash or recalibration. I'm also adjusting the Hampel filter's scale floor to account for quantization.

Actually, maybe not worth it—the inflated outlier count is just a symptom, so I'll skip touching filter behavior and just report it instead.

For calibration, I'm thinking compute_calibration should add warnings when steps show low-resolution frames, plus a csi_resolution block in the result, and CalibrationManager.save should refuse low-quality saves unless the caller confirms, with the UI surfacing those warnings and a "save anyway" option—something the coder can implement after checking current UI save behavior. I'll leave the quiet_p95 threshold fallback as is.

For raw recording during calibration, I'm working out that CalibrationManager should spin up a dedicated recording session per placement when running against a live source, recording each calibration step as its own labeled take (empty_baseline, walking, standing_still, sitting), with start/stop triggered by the CalibrationSession's state transitions—though this requires careful coordination since those transitions happen on the engine thread while the recorder also writes there, so the coder will need to design proper hooks and store the resulting session/take IDs in the raw_recording field of the calibration result.

I also want an offline diagnose CLI (`python -m backend.cli diagnose`) that takes a recording session or file plus an optional calibration, runs it through SignalProcessor, and reports packet rate, amplitude stats, motion score distributions, and posture classification if available—backed by a Makefile target and a small real-data fixture for testing low-resolution detection.

Now I'm shifting into FEAT-004, the posture feature.

Adding a "moving" class derived from walking step profiles, extending the class set and state mapping so moving gets its own state while the Fisher-based sit-vs-stand split and self-check logic stay compatible with older models. For PostureClassifier, I want high-confidence "moving" window classifications to transition directly into the moving state via the existing confirm-timer logic, and I'm considering an out-of-distribution check based on per-subcarrier log-likelihood against the calibration.

I'm calibrating an OOD threshold from training data by computing each still class's own-class log-likelihood and setting a floor below the 1st percentile; at runtime, if the best still-class likelihood falls below this floor, I classify as moving (when motion score supports it) or otherwise flag as unknown with a clear "doesn't match any calibrated posture" reason rather than ever defaulting to sitting.

I also want window-level instability checks comparing the spread of per-frame profiles against the still-class variance, plus tests using synthetic noisy walking profiles to confirm the classifier correctly returns moving instead of sitting even when the motion score dips low, along with a regression test replaying the original failure case where thresholds aren't separable.
